info.bio:
Motörhead fue una banda icono del hard rock inglés. Fundada por el ex bajista de Hawkwind, Lemmy Kilmister.

Normalmente denominada como un power trio, Motörhead en los años 1980 tuvo un gran éxito con muchos singles en los UK Top 40 chart. Los álbumes 'Overkill', 'Bomber', 'Ace of Spades' y, particularmente, 'No Sleep 'tal Hammersmith', dan a Motörhead la reputación de una las mejores bandas de heavy metal británico.

Mientras que la banda es clasificada comúnmente como heavy metal o speed metal (y, a menudo, considerado como una influencia fundamental en los dos últimos estilos), Kilmister ha rechazado tales etiquetas prefiriendo describir el estilo de Motörhead como "rock and roll".

Lemmy manifestó que generalmente se encontraba más afín al punk rock que a las bandas de heavy metal. Motörhead tocó en conciertos con The Damned, con quienes Lemmy había tocado el bajo en una serie de conciertos de finales de los años 70, y había escrito la canción "R.A.M.O.N.E.S." como homenaje a Ramones. Lemmy decía que Motörhead tenía más similitudes estéticas con The Damned que con Black Sabbath y nada en común con Judas Priest. Además la banda hizo una versión de la canción "God Save the Queen" de Sex Pistols. Aseguraba no tener nada en común con las bandas de speed metal a las que Motörhead ha influido.

Entre los temas más conocidos de Motörhead están "Ace of Spades", que se refiere a la vida de un jugador de cartas que prefiere llevar una vida intensa a una tranquila y aburrida, "Overkill", "Orgasmatron", "Born to Raise Hell" o "Bite the Bullet". Motörhead ha sido referente del metal desde su aparición hace más de 30 años, influenciando a bandas como Metallica o Sepultura, quienes han declarado públicamente su admiración por este trío.

Durante agosto de 2005, cuando celebraban sus 30 años de carrera artística, se lanzó un documental titulado "Live Fast, Die Old", y en el 2006 su sello Sanctuary Records lanzó "Kiss of Death", sucesor de "Infierno" (2004).

La banda se disolvió con la muerte de Lemmy el 28 de diciembre de 2015. . User-contributed text is available under the Creative Commons By-SA License; additional terms may apply.

own_scenes.desc: Lemmy Kilmister venía de la banda psicodélica Hawkwind y en 1976 forma Motörhead, un grupo rápido y muy pesado que tomó el nombre de una canción de Hawkwind y la versionó: la comparación entre original y versión muestra que el heavy no continúa la psicodelia sino que irrumpe. Llevan el elemento rítmico del heavy al extremo y son uno de los modelos de los que surge el thrash. «Rock ’n’ Roll» celebra la música porque da sentido a la vida.

refs.q: Lemmy Kilmister, originally with a British psychedelic band called Hawkwind, began Motörhead in 1976.
refs.para: Further evidence of the influence of psychedelic music on heavy metal is provided by artists who shifted from that style of music to heavy metal. Lemmy Kilmister, originally with a British psychedelic band called Hawkwind, began Motörhead in 1976. Motörhead is a fast and very heavy metal outfit that is still going strong. The band’s name was taken from a Hawkwind song, which it covered. Comparison of the original and the cover show that heavy metal is not continuous with psychedelic music, but a genuine eruption, even if it borrows elements from this predecessor. In the United States Ted Nugent also made the switch from psychedelic to heavy metal music. His band, Amboy Dukes, was a psychedelic group, with a 1969 hit song “Journey to the Center of Your Mind.” Nugent’s change was more gradual than Kilmister’s, but by 1976, with the release of Free for All, he was squarely in the heavy metal camp. The relationship between heavy metal and hard psychedelia can also be traced with reference to Uriah Heep. Their first album in 1970 and most of their subsequent material (they, too, are still around) fall within psychedelia. But several of their songs fit clearly within the heavy metal genre. A few commentators even classify Uriah Heep as a heavy metal band. Mike Saunders, reviewing a Uriah Heep album for Rolling Stone in 1972, argued for the band’s transitional position; their vocals are “psychedelic,” he said, but “the guitar and rhythm section is English heavy metal rock.”¹⁴
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: the melodic and rhythmic elements were taken to extremes by the Scorpions and Motorhead, respectively
refs.para: By 1983–84 two major subgenres were in place. Each emphasized a different feature of traditional heavy metal. One of them privileged the melody and the other stressed the rhythm. Heavy metal bands in the 1970s may have emphasized one of these musical elements more than the other, but they were heard and judged within the overall code of the genre. For example, the melodic and rhythmic elements were taken to extremes by the Scorpions and Motorhead, respectively. These bands were understood to be working out the possibilities within the genre’s code, rather than challenging or attempting to alter it. In the 1970s no segregation of styles in terms of concert bookings, fans, and fanzines was apparent. All this changed during the 1980s. It was as if traditional heavy metal was a solution of various elements that finally became supersaturated and began to crystallize. The fragmentation of the 1980s included a lyrical as well as a musical component split: the melodic specialization took up the Dionysian legacy whereas the more rhythmically oriented level closed ranks around the legacy of Chaos.

scenes.name: La radio: del exilio a Z-Rock
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Durante su primera década el heavy casi no suena en la radio: la FM progresiva rechaza a Black Sabbath por cambiar «love» por «evil», el AOR de los consultores solo pone «Stairway to Heaven» y algo de AC/DC, y a los anunciantes no les interesan los chicos de quince a dieciocho años. Weinstein ve ventajas en ese exilio: obliga a las bandas a girar sin parar (Aerosmith, Blue Öyster Cult y Ted Nugent, más de cuarenta semanas al año), las une a su público, las libra de los códigos radiofónicos (canciones de ocho minutos como «War Pigs», solos largos, el disco y no el single como unidad) y explica la abundancia de discos en directo. En los ochenta llegan los programas de metal en las radios universitarias (WSOU de Seton Hall se pasa entera al metal), el informe metal de CMJ y su Metal Marathon, y en la radio comercial el formato por satélite Z-Rock desde Dallas, que relega el thrash a su «Headbanger’s Heaven» nocturno. En Gran Bretaña, el único refugio es el «Friday Night Rock Show» de la BBC con Tommy Vance. Cuando la radio comercial acepta el metal es a través de MTV y de las power ballads, y exige productores de éxitos y solos recortados; aun así Metallica vende un millón de …And Justice for All sin apenas sonar.

scenes.name: La edad de oro del heavy metal
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El heavy metal renace en los mismos años que la new wave, aprovechando los sellos independientes: Motörhead (puente entre metal, Stooges/MC5 y punk), Judas Priest, Iron Maiden, Diamond Head, Def Leppard y, en EE UU, Van Halen. Entre 1982 y 1985 el subgénero gótico se convierte en «black metal» (Venom, Mercyful Fate, Celtic Frost, Helloween, Bathory). El pop-metal y el shock-rock (Twisted Sister, Mötley Crüe, Joan Jett, Bon Jovi, Savatage); la pompa y el doom (Manowar, Voivod, Saint Vitus, Pentagram); el metal progresivo (Living Colour, Queensrÿche, King's X, Pantera, Joe Satriani) y el «street sound» de Los Ángeles (Guns N' Roses, Jane's Addiction, Faster Pussycat).

podcast.title: Extreme Volume Causes Structural Damage (1986)
podcast.body: In 1986, Motörhead reportedly achieved a volume of 130 decibels during a gig, a level so intense that it "caused structural damage to the variety, theater and cleveland." This event further pushed the boundaries of live concert volume. "Later it was claimed that Motorhead hit 130 decibels in 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Adoption of the "Rock Dot" Umlaut
podcast.body: Motörhead famously adopted the umlaut (or "rock dot") in their name, contributing to the association of these diacritics with metal bands, primarily for their cool, foreign, or menacing aesthetic. "There's Motley Crew, Queen's Reich, Spinal Tap, Green Jelly, Motorhead, Maximal Park, Moxie Frouze, and tons of others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Axis Memorabilia Collection
podcast.body: During his lifetime, Lemmy Kilmister was known for his collection of memorabilia from Axis countries of World War II, which included items from Germany, Hungary, and Italy. "he collected material from all the Axis countries of World War II. So Germany, yes, but also Hungary, Italy, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band T-Shirt Etiquette
podcast.body: Motorhead t-shirts were specifically mentioned in the context of people wearing band shirts bought from "fast fashion places" without knowing anything about the band. "They've got a Motorhead or Nirvana shirt."

podcast.title: Fan Injury from Headbanging
podcast.body: A 50-year-old German man developed a subdural hematoma after enthusiastically headbanging at a Motörhead show a month prior to his symptoms. Doctors performed surgery to remove the blood clot, and he recovered, with headbanging identified as the likely cause. "He'd been to a motor head show a month earlier and had been enthusiastically banging his head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lemmy's Roadie Past
podcast.body: Lemmy Kilmister, the frontman for Motorhead, had personal experience as a roadie, having worked for Jimi Hendrix by "humping gear" before he began his performing career. This background made him uniquely sympathetic to the role and efforts of road crews. "Lemmy is uniquely sympathetic to road crews because he himself used to hump gear for Jimmy Hendrix before he moved on to performing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

podcast.title: Major Influence on UK Hardcore
podcast.body: Motörhead was identified as the biggest influence from the New Wave of British Heavy Metal scene on UK Hardcore, which itself was an amalgamation of British punk and NWOBHM. "The biggest influence from that scene was Motorhead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Managed by Sharon Osborne
podcast.body: Motörhead were among the clients managed by Sharon Osborne, daughter of the old-school manager Don Arden. Osborne's management career encompassed a range of heavy rock and metal acts.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ongoing Re-edition & Remastering Campaign
podcast.body: Much of Motörhead's material has been undergoing re-editing and remastering in recent years, with the process still incomplete. This ongoing effort indicates a comprehensive revisiting of their discography. "también se está reditando mucho material en los últimos años de motorgén, aún no está todo reditado y remasterizado."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Record Store Day 2018. Resumen de lanzamientos.

podcast.title: Origin of "Headbanging" Term
podcast.body: According to Lemmy, the term "headbanging" was derived from the name of his band, suggesting a direct link such as "Motörhead banging." The band's fast songs, some reaching 200 beats per minute, put extreme strain on the neck. "Then if you had talked to Lemmy, he would say that the term head banging was derived from the name of his band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Motorhead is among the rock acts that have released their own line of sex toys. "Also, Guar, Mothly Crew, Ghost, Motorhead, No Effects, which is an inflatable sheep, if you must ask, and appropriately the English punk band, the vibrators."

podcast.title: Thrash Metal Pioneer
podcast.body: Motorhead is mentioned as an example of a thrash metal band, a style that blended hardcore punk aggression with metal's sound, characterized by faster and harder playing. "So I think Slayer, Motorhead, Megadeath, and Anthrax."

xref.title: Mighty Mighty Bosstones – Formed 1983 Boston; Invented Skacore by Mixing Two-Tone with Hardcore; Major Label by 1993
xref.body: The Mighty Mighty Bosstones came together in 1983 when a group of guys became obsessed with the Two-Tone sound despite some members playing in hardcore bands influenced by Motorhead and AC/DC. This combination of Two-Tone ska with American hardcore became known as skacore — annoying to ska purists and initially baffling to hardcore kids, but eventually it clicked. By 1993 they had a major label record deal and a signature look involving plaid suits. "The Boss Tones took two-tone style Skah and made it with American hardcore to create something that was eventually called Skahcore."

xref.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
xref.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. All kinds of people came to pay their respects, including Lemmy of Motorhead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Musical Education – Self-Taught with Records and Pillows
xref.body: Dave Grohl grew up in Washington D.C., where he learned to play drums and guitar by meticulously studying records from bands like KISS, Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, Black Flag, The Stooges, and Motorhead. While he took guitar lessons first, he taught himself drums by arranging pillows on his bed and practicing with borrowed sticks. "he learned the drums by arranging pillows on his bed and banging them with some borrowed sticks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exile to England
xref.body: Following a violent confrontation related to his drug activities and a brush with the law, Dillon's parents gave him an ultimatum to leave Kingston, which he signed an agreement not to return to for several years. He traveled to England, his first time on a plane or subway, where he busked, squatted, and famously drank with Lemmy from Motörhead, resolving to pursue music instead of a life of crime. "So I got on a plane. I went to England, never been on a plane in my life, never been on a subway."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Failed Petition for Heavy Metal Element
xref.body: A petition to name a heavy metal element after Lemmy of Motorhead failed. The primary reasons were that scientific rules for naming new elements do not allow for musicians as sources, only mythological concepts, minerals, places, countries, properties, or scientists. Additionally, the new "heavy" elements (113, 115, 117, 118) are actually classified as non-metals on the periodic table. "This petition was inspired by the idea that an actual heavy metal element be named after Lemmy and with atomic weights between 113 and 118, these new elements are the heaviest yet discovered. Perfect. Awesome. Sounds great. However, if we look at the periodic table, you'll see that these new elements occupy space on the right hand side. This is the area of the table reserved for non-metals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Flamboyance and Influence
xref.body: Despite performing as a Black and gay artist in the US South in the 1950s, Little Richard's flamboyance, energy, and music had a massive effect across rock and roll. His influence extended to artists like The Beatles, James Brown, David Bowie, and even Lemmy of Motorhead, reverberating through the entire genre. "His flamboyance, his energy, and his music reverberated through all of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Rock Music
xref.body: The Ramones are credited with profoundly influencing countless rock bands over several decades, with a direct lineage tracing back to their original version for bands like Rise Against, Metallica, Blink 182, Motorhead, Green Day, Guns N' Roses, The Clash, Sex Pistols, Rancid, The Pixies, The Beastie Boys, Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, The Strokes, The Offspring, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. "virtually any rock band of the last 25 years, 35 years, and you can draw a line back into the past, and that line will inevitably lead back to the Ramones."

xref.title: Rainbow Bar & Grill Tribute
xref.body: Lemmy Kilmister was a regular patron at The Rainbow Bar & Grill on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles. Following his death, the venue preserved his favorite chair at the end of the bar as a permanent tribute. Patrons can also order "a Lemmy," which is his preferred drink of Jack Daniel's and Coke. "Lemmy of Motorhead was a fixture at a venue called the Rainbow in Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles. After he died, they preserved his favorite chair at the end of the bar as a tribute. You can also order a drink in the bar called a Lemmy, which is favorite drink, Jack Daniels and Coke."

xref.title: Roadie for Jimi Hendrix
xref.body: Before becoming a performer with Motorhead, Lemmy Kilmister worked as a roadie for Jimi Hendrix, where he was responsible for "humping gear." This personal experience gave him a unique understanding and sympathy for road crews. "Lemmy is uniquely sympathetic to road crews because he himself used to hump gear for Jimmy Hendrix before he moved on to performing."

xref.title: Third Wave Pioneers
xref.body: Formed in 1983 in Boston, The Mighty Mighty Bosstones were early practitioners of the third wave of Ska, initially inspired by the Two Tone movement but also incorporating hard rock influences from bands like ACDC, Motorhead, and Social Distortion. They became prominent in the late 1980s and early 1990s by fusing Ska with hardcore elements. "The Mighty Mighty Boss Tones. They were formed in 1983 and inspired by the whole two-tone thing, at least originally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Thrash Metal Pioneer
xref.body: Slayer is cited as an example of a thrash metal band, a genre that emerged as hardcore punk influenced metal, leading to faster and harder music. "So I think Slayer, Motorhead, Megadeath, and Anthrax."
